summary:
This evaluation covers 19 SageMaker-security chat evals run 3x each on both variants (99 total iterations, 1 failed run). Five evals were marked should_trigger:false and fully skipped (no data to compare), so the comparison rests on the remaining 14 evals.

**Trigger firing:** Both variants fired the expected behavior 100% of the time across all evals where this was measured — not a differentiator.

**Expected output / assertions — the dominant pattern:** Across nearly every eval, with_skill met the expected output far more often than without_skill, often 100% vs 0%, and this is backed by high-confidence judgments in most cases (a couple were medium confidence). At the assertion level, the same pattern repeats heavily: many individual assertions show "with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails," particularly ones requiring a "Verifiability classification" label on findings — this specific requirement was missed by without_skill in eval after eval (sm-13, sm-17, sm-04, sm-18/19, schema-shape, sm22-manual-approval, etc.), suggesting a systematic formatting/compliance gap for without_skill rather than isolated misses. A few assertions passed for both variants equally ("always_passes," e.g., mentioning AccessDenied, naming specific roles/APIs), showing some underlying content recognition is shared between variants and not itself a distinguishing capability. One assertion ("Approval lineage actions" in sm22-manual-approval) failed for both variants, indicating that specific check is not working for either and may need rework regardless of variant. A few assertions were flagged "flaky" (inconsistent results within a variant's own repeated runs), notably in owns-vs-defers, sm18/19, and sm17-live evals, meaning those particular measurements are less reliable regardless of which variant is stronger.

Two evals (sm13-job-definitions, sm17-local-storage, sm04-suspended-detector) show without_skill matching with_skill on expected-output pass rate (3/3) while still losing on finalized assertion detail (e.g., missing the Verifiability label), so the overall outcome of "met expected output" and the finer per-assertion grading sometimes diverge — the aggregate expected-output pass rate alone would hide where exactly without_skill fell short.

**Runtime and cost:** Results are mixed and don't track a consistent direction. In some evals with_skill was much slower and more expensive (e.g., sagemaker-sec-assessment: with_skill 1m42s/$0.85 vs without_skill 3m39s/$1.82 — here without_skill was actually slower/costlier) while in others without_skill was faster/cheaper (e.g., sagemaker-sec-schema-shape: with_skill 1m46s/$0.88 vs without_skill 3m48s/$1.90, again without_skill slower here) — actually across most evals, with_skill tends to run longer and cost more in simpler evals (8s vs 0s, 13s vs 8s) while in the two heaviest/longest evals (sagemaker-sec-assessment, schema-shape) without_skill is markedly slower and costlier than with_skill. So no single consistent cost/speed direction holds across the board; the pattern varies by eval.

**Quality comparison (head-to-head judged pairs):** Most evals skipped quality pairwise comparison (pairs_skipped), limiting how much can be said here. Where pairs were evaluated (sagemaker-sec-read-only, sm13-job-definitions, sm17-local-storage, sm04-suspended-detector, sm18/19-local-storage), with_skill was favored more often than without_skill overall, though in sm17-local-storage and sm04-suspended-detector the margin was fairly close (4 vs 3, and 5 vs 3, with some "comparable" judgments), and confidence on these was often medium. This is a real but not overwhelming signal in with_skill's favor on quality where it could be measured, and it only covers a subset of evals.

**Output consistency (run-to-run stability):** Variant_a's outputs were "consistent" or "mostly_consistent" in nearly all evals where consistency was assessed, with one exception (sagemaker-sec-owns-vs-defers, where with_skill was rated "inconsistent"). Variant_b's consistency was more mixed, including "inconsistent" ratings in sm22-manual-approval and sm17-live, and several nulls where it couldn't be assessed. This suggests with_skill's outputs were somewhat more stable run-to-run in this eval set, though both variants had at least one instance of low stability.

**Overall picture:** The most consistent and highest-confidence signal across this eval set is that with_skill met the defined expected-output criteria and individual assertions substantially more often than without_skill, especially around a recurring "Verifiability classification" labeling requirement that without_skill repeatedly missed. Where quality was directly compared head-to-head, with_skill was favored more often, though this comparison only covered a handful of evals and confidence was sometimes medium. Runtime/cost show no consistent direction — both variants were faster/cheaper than the other in different evals. A handful of assertions failed for both variants or were flaky for both, indicating some test criteria themselves may need refinement independent of which variant is used. Five negative-trigger evals were skipped entirely and contribute no comparative data.
</summary>

This means with_skill's outputs varied more from run to run, even though it passed more assertions and met the expected output more often on average — so its stronger pass rates came with less run-to-run reliability, while without_skill was more consistent but consistently missed more checks.

In sum: with_skill shows higher (but still low, ~33%) expected-output and assertion pass rates with high-confidence measurements, while without_skill is faster, cheaper, and more consistent across repeated runs but fails more of the specific assertions and the expected output check entirely in this sample.
